Unable to bear it, he came forth and said: "Within the ocean of dust-motes and *kṣetras*, there are ten kinds of extraordinary things; these are indeed all known. But among them, is there one thing that does not enter into the count? Do you know it or not? To this, one need only say to him: [The following verse: "Ten thousand years of cultivation, yet still not knowing the root; A single moment of thought, and the myriad phenomena are all revealed. If you wish to see the Buddha, look at the person before you; If you wish to hear the Dharma, listen to your own voice. He asked again: "What is this 'person'? Boarding the boat, we compare our baskets.
On the first day of the fourth month, I ascend the hall: Yesterday I saw off spring’s departure; this morning I welcome the beginning of summer.

A single tree, perhaps two trees, of fading blossoms; the cuckoo calls three times, then four. All these are clearly transcendent of sound and form—how many are still asleep and have not yet awakened? *A!* (Silence)
I lay bare my very heart and soul to you all.
Tonight, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, I offer thanks to those who have shared this path with me as I ascend the hall. The clouds part to the north of the hermitage; the moon bathes the eastern isles.

Those who point at it, talk about it, or gaze upon it mostly end up failing to appreciate this fine autumn. This mountain monk, however, tonight shall walk hand-in-hand with you. (He strikes the meditation staff.)
It is said: "Wiping it away, it transcends Yunmen’s 'Six Non-Attainments.

On the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall: "For six years I sat in emaciation, enduring hunger and cold; How laughable, that I turned my back on them and emerged from the mountains once more.
It was simply that there was no fixed vision before my eyes; Last night, I was deceived by a single star."
The Preface for the Opening Ceremony of Shouputong Guang Chan Temple, compiled by Attendant Shixun.
The Prime Minister originally had no private interests; he merely disliked the "Fujianese. Holding up the petition, he said: "This alone is just like..."
The names are written upon the wall; as for how the original text within them should be cited, the *Dudu shu* says: "The white surface is the paper;
the black surface is the characters."
Ascending the seat, he delivered this discourse: "Ten thousand acres of misty waves; a single sky of wind and moon. A thousand-fathom line hangs straight down;
with a single flick of the hand, six great turtles are lightly hauled up. Is there anyone who does not covet the fragrant bait? (The question and answer are not recorded).
The General Outline: To him we must grant a person of transcendent measure; he upholds matters of transcendent measure.

Occupying the great seat, he remains composed and at ease, like a green horse standing across the stable, towering over the ravines and reaching toward the heavens. He unleashes the Great Function through direct confrontation and lateral guidance, causing the compassionate stream to overflow with verdant waves.
Surging to the heavens and washing over the sun, the scales of authority are held in hand; gathering and releasing are entirely at one's own will. Yet, little do they realize:
the qilin within the moon gazes upon the Northern Dipper, and by the walls of the King of Chu’s city, the waters flow eastward.

A-he-he! What is this? Kāśyapa did not transmit it; Bodhidharma did not recognize it. (He strikes the meditation staff once. The spring-like harmony of a single breath turns the great forge; the clouds clear from the eight vast reaches as the realm of longevity opens.
The following day, he ascended the hall for the Chancellor, Duke of Guo. With great wisdom, he penetrated all things clearly; throughout the ten directions, his influence flowed unimpeded.

Relying on the power of his vows, he propagated the profound Dharma; he established meritorious achievements in this sagely age. As a general abroad and a minister within, he turned the celestial and terrestrial spheres to create anew;

as a regulator of the primal essence and a mender of the imperial robes, he raised the sun and moon to the center of heaven. Now, as he controls his crane and roams in spirit, in which realm does he ultimately dwell?
The ground. Where the nine lotuses open and close, the hundred jewels naturally adorn it.
Entering the hall, [the Master] raised a case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa? Yunmen said, "I do not understand. The monk pressed further: "..."
"Why is it that one cannot understand? Yunmen said, "Simply by guarding [the mind], one cannot understand. The Master said, "Yunmen spoke of 'not being able to understand' once more;
this can be called having a thorn in the mud. Suddenly, if someone were to ask Kaishou, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?
he would simply say to him, "Recognize that which cannot be understood."
Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: It cannot be known by the intellect, nor can it be recognized by consciousness. Last night the first yang arose;
this morning it is the twenty-first day. Every blossom of the plum tree plays with the colors of spring.
On the Lantern Festival, he moved to the mountain gate and ascended the hall. "One lamp is bright; from lamp to lamp, they are inexhaustible. One gate opens; in gate after gate, there is a path.
He struck his staff once and said, "Look, look! The ancient Buddha of the bright lamp is currently beneath the feet of you all."
The earth shakes and light is emitted; the staff of Deshan is broken and the shout of Linji silenced.
I require you all, without moving a single step, to ascend directly to the stage of Buddhahood through this very gate. Should you hesitate, the ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he entered Hangzhou. Again, wearing yellow robes, he ascended the hall: "The Buddha’s face is yellow; my body’s robes are yellow.
The stars shift and the constellations turn; it is like adding frost to snow. *Aha!* Living on the mountain is as busy as leaving the mountain.
While reading the *Qingmiao jing* (Sūtra of the Green Sprouts) in the Central Lands, I also offer thanks to Jiweng, Wushun, Shangyin, and the three Tripitaka masters for their presence in the hall.
Half of this summer has already passed; this matter must be resolved. Even now, expounding upon the Great Canon and the Small Canon is still merely dwelling in emptiness to speak of emptiness.
But tell me, what is ultimate emptiness? [He strikes the meditation staff once. Let the vast ocean flow as it will.
[The Master] transformed [the situation]. He would never act as an intermediary for the ruler.

On the full moon of the sixth month, he ascended the hall, took up his staff, and called to the assembly, saying: "All sentient beings of this great earth are in a state of restless turmoil and profound confusion."
Chaos and confusion everywhere. This mountain monk cannot bear to witness it. Amidst the blazing heat of the sixth month, he plants his staff and says:
"With a single crash of thunder, the rain pours down like a basin being overturned, so that the three kinds of grasses and two kinds of trees are all moistened by its nourishment.
Do you all feel your spirits refreshed and your breath clear? He leans on the staff and says: "Ants do not eat iron."

Ascending the hall: The three months of spring have drawn to a close; the foliage is deep green and the blossoms sparse. Movement turns one toward external objects; stillness leads to delusion regarding the Dharma.
Do not be obscured by form; do not be mounted upon sound. Before the breeze, listen idly to the cry of the cuckoo.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Each thing does not know the other; each dharma is not like the other. The autumn waters are clear as glass; the autumn mountains reveal their bare bones.
Ruiyan calls out to the master of the house, yet he himself is not awake. Magu carries a hoe into the garden, stealing away his body to perform manual labor."
The elders of old toyed with the spirits and souls of ghosts, leading their descendants of later generations to lose the path for turning back.
*Aha!* You head toward West Qin; I go to East Lu.
On a spring day, rising from illness, he ascended the hall. He cited an ancient worthy who said: "When there is a self, my illness arises;
when there is no self, my illness ceases. When both self and illness are absent, ten thousand miles away is but a single bar of iron.

He added: "There is yet one final phrase; I shall explain it to you all in due course. He then offered this verse: "Moss covers the ground, elm coins fill the earth; The courtyard is empty, willow catkins drift."
He flies off. Turning the pages at random, the incense seals grow cold; the evening mountain’s green hues ascend the window frames.
Entering the hall, he said: "Deshan and Linji carried out their commands to the full; Yantou and Xuefeng expounded the Dharma to the full.
Yet, if one examines them closely, they too only managed to speak of a single fragment. Why is this? In the sixth month it does not get hot; the five grains do not ripen."
Compiled by the Attendant De Gao and Hui Zhu of Daochang Chan Monastery in Huzhou. The waters of the Shao River ripple;
the cloud-peaks embrace their splendor. To directly take up the responsibility—to push open the door and enter the mortar.
In the Buddha Hall (where the Buddha has not yet been enshrined), the past is already past; the future is yet to come. Where does the present reside?
Striking the incense burner, he says: "For the most part, people miss it right before their own faces."
Taking his place in the hall, he held his staff horizontally across his chest and said, "This is for those of middling and lower capacity. But what if a person of the highest caliber were to come?
[He leaned the staff against it] and said: 'A fierce tiger does not eat meat that has already been lying there.'"
The Preface by the President states: "Every word reveals the ultimate truth; every sentence points toward the source. The Preface by Du states: "The wind follows the tiger;
the clouds follow the dragon."
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said: "Producing excellence in the land of Central Wu, its fragrance flows through the ancient site of practice.

It spans across the seventy-two peaks of Mount Nanyue and rises prominently from the ten-thousand-eight-hundred-foot heights of Mount Huading. To meet face-to-face at this critical moment, I take this fragrant offering and pray for the longevity of the sovereign and the endurance of the realm."
The General Outline: The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū is utterly beyond names and models. He sat upon the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet, as time passed, things became stale.
The Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he fell short by a mere fraction, failing to attain the Way of Buddhahood.

To see the whole of reality directly—this mountain monk has already revealed each and every sublime teaching of the ancient Buddhas to you all. Nevertheless, the clouds and the moon are one and the same.
Valleys and mountains each differ. It is just like two mountains with a single gate that controls your path of entry.
You people, having already reached the clear pool beneath the eaves, have you ever seen fire burning within the water?

If you can see it, then you walk hand-in-hand with the Patriarch, traversing tiger dens at will; holding the reins and applying the pressure, gathering and releasing with total freedom. Now tell me: what is the "Correct" [Way]?
At such a time, after all, by whose power of grace is one sustained? The heavens are high and the myriad creatures face their proper direction;
the seas are vast and the hundred rivers flow toward them. Again, it is said: When the Venerable Buddhāpālī arrived at Mount Wutai, an old man asked him, "Where have you come from?"
The Venerable One said, "I have come from India. The Old Man asked, "Have you brought the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya Sūtra* with you?
The Venerable One replied, "I have not brought it. [The Master] commented: "O Assembly! When the Old Man asked thus, he certainly had not yet reached India.
When the Venerable One answered thus, was this not that very scroll? Let those with eyes discern this!"
Ascending the hall: When Mazu ascended the hall, the turtle bit the fishing rod; when Baizhang rolled up his mat, the snake gripped the rat’s tail.
Thus, father and son joined hands to uphold the Great Teaching with all their might. Yet, alas, it is difficult to deceive the eyes of the multitude.
What is this matter that is so difficult to deceive? The frosty moon reaches the door and the chessboard grows cold; the water and clouds enshroud the rocks as the monk’s robe feels chill.
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: "In the Western Heaven, the retreat was commenced with a wax man as the verification. At Huya Rock, what is used as the verification?
[He] strikes the meditation staff and says: "Seizing the tiger's head and gathering in the tiger's tail."
Ascending the hall, he said: "It cannot be known by wisdom; it cannot be recognized by consciousness. Last night the golden wind turned;
this morning is the first day of the seventh month. Cast away the 'one,' pick up the 'seven. Ten thousand acres of grain turn with the autumn colors."
Ascending the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat, he struck his staff and said: "The arena of perfect enlightenment is opened. Again, striking his staff, he said: "Release the water buffalo;
without rope or tether, it goes and stays as it pleases. A single note from the cross-flute: heaven and earth are autumn."
Ascending the hall, the mountain monk was so impoverished that he had not even a single awl; yet one night, suddenly, he became wealthy.
Pine needles were transformed into golden hairpins, and flakes of ice turned into pieces of jade. Now that these treasures are manifest before you, who among the thieves could possibly steal them?
Even Śākyamuni and Maitreya, or Deshan and Linji—these would still be mere bandits dividing up the loot. Tell me, which of these is the true one?
“Thief! [The Master] gave a shout.
He then ascended the hall to express his gratitude to Head Seat Shaoming and the Attendant of Lingyin. “Thirty years ago, we traveled together; the clouds and moon were shared by us both.
Thirty years later, it is unbearable to converse with them; the streams and mountains have each become different. This is the Buddha-dharma of the Patriarchs.”
Zen. Set it aside to one side. Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout—neither has any use here. Why?
Because the National Teacher struck his attendant, and Nanquan slew the cat.

Ascending the hall on the fifteenth day of the intercalary fourth month: I have already seen the fifteenth day of the fourth month, and I see it again—layer upon layer, like drawing lines on the ground to mark a prison, still further reinforced by casting in solid iron.

If you possess eyes that penetrate the barrier, you may go about your business with unconcerned strides; yet if this is not yet the case, only when you step upon it will you know it is not as it seems.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Head Seat for holding the whisk and the Chief Administrator for preparing the meal. As he sat, he drew in the fragrant breeze blowing from the south;

how joyful! In that single moment, he attained sudden enlightenment. Having personally received the phrase that brings true power, he has fully sated himself with the flavor of *amṛta*. Everything is vividly clear, left unrevealed and unhidden.
Lifting his tongue three thousand miles, he enters the new Sangha Hall.
Hanging the plaque upon the hall, he manifests a precious monastery amidst a heap of rubble. He specially inscribes the new plaque, opening the field for the selection of Buddhas.
Beholding it before one’s eyes, its silver hooks and iron strokes are clear; looking up at its ever-higher form, the phoenix soars and the dragon ascends.
Xiang! To live among people with earnest sincerity, to be luminous and without concealment—to arrive as one who possesses the eye, to directly accept the responsibility at once.
With every step taken, one treads firmly; a single tile laid upon a patch of ground. With every glance raised, one verifies everything;

a single pillar supporting a single beam. In responding to conditions there is precision; in wondrous adaptation there is no fixed method. From within this, the chosen continue the life of wisdom for ten thousand generations.

World-Honored One, by this prayer, may you open the realm of longevity throughout the eight directions. How laughable are those who, their strength exhausted and their path at its end, merely bow their heads and enter;

and how laughable are those who, when the branch grows outside the joint, have the Oxherd circle the hall. Just as on this auspicious day, the eighteenth, we mark this plaque in accordance with the ritual.
And enter this hall. You people, how will you embody and take charge? [The Master] strikes his staff once.
He cites Chan Master Huanglong Nan, who entered the Sangha Hall together with Chan Master Longqing Xian. Nan said, "A fine Sangha hall."
Qingyun said, "The meditation hall is fine. Longtan asked, "In what way is it fine? Qingyun replied, "One beam faces one pillar.
Longtan pointed his finger and said, "This pillar is so round; that beam is so flat. Qingyun said, [It is so.]
"A person who is a teacher of gods and humans does not lack a *upādhyāya*. Huanglong [Huinan] picked up the case and said:

"When these two great elders, Huanglong and Longqing, exchanged such questions and answers, it was like wrapping a stone in brocade or encasing a weight in cotton. Suppose someone were to ask today, 'What about a fine monk's hall? I would say to him:
'Last year, on the day of Gengshen in the twelfth lunar month, the wooden pillars were erected; this year, on the day of Jiwu in the ninth lunar month, they returned to the hall.'"
On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "An ancient worthy said, 'The entire earth is bright and clear;
where there is even a single thread, there is that very thread—there is seizing and there is releasing. The entire earth is bright and clear;

where there is even a single thread, there is not a single thread—there is total letting go and total withdrawal. Do you all know where these two great elders have landed? (He remained silent for a long while.)"
It is said: "Fortunately, it is as level as a mirror; what need is there for it to be curved like a hook?
When the letter from Master Yunfeng of Jingshan arrived, [the Master] ascended the hall to transmit the Mind-essence of the Buddha and propagate the Way of the Buddha’s Wisdom.
He also said, "To dwell on the summit" and "to attain abiding. Throughout his life, he spoke horizontally and vertically, yet no one could comprehend the ultimate point.
The latter phrase: "He went to the Dharma hall and beat his breast with his hands. Why? Because words of bitter grievance are not easily uttered.
Returning to the Hall once more due to these circumstances: "In the spring confluence, the river returns the pearl; its brilliant, cold radiance pierces the great void."
Held aloft by a single hand, it cannot be shattered; the moon remains bright, ascending the coral tree.

On this occasion of the Imperial Birthday, I ascend the hall. Most expansive and most vast, most noble and most supreme—like the moon traveling through the sky, the great earth is entirely encompassed by its single illumination;
like water in the sea, a thousand waves merge into a single source. This humble monk today offers praise; I praise!
Sighing that it cannot be reached, he suddenly grasps his staff and says, "Now listen to this staff as it comes forth to join us in offering congratulations and praise.
He strikes once and says:
"May auspiciousness unfold on the birthday of the Heavenly Longevity, surpassing ten million myriad years."
At Zhongxia, he ascended the hall and raised the following case: Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying, "Today marks the end of the summer retreat.
Bring forth a word that strikes home. The assembly was speechless. Yunmen then said, "Mitrā-jñāna. [The Master] commented: "How great is Yunmen!"
Presenting this Sanskrit verse to others, I teach them how it should be understood: Rent and taxes arrive at the granary every morning;
When asked about the harvest, they say it is difficult to sustain. The waterwheel stands idle outside the green willows; Under the blazing sun, the young seedlings wither.
He was bestowed with a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya* and the honorary title of Master Foxhai Xingkong.

Upon ascending the hall to express his gratitude for this imperial favor, he established the definitive orthodox lineage. Specifically granted the gold-embroidered dharma robes and further conferred the honorary title "Manifesting and Exalting the Ocean-like Nature of Emptiness," he received full and profound honor.
Like the wind following the tiger and the clouds following the dragon, his virtue moved the Emperor above.
How can the Imperial Grace be repaid? The Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands upon Mount Zhurong. Entering the hall, he said:
"On this day of the *jiǎzǐ* cycle in autumn, rain falls and ears grow upon the heads of the grain. The waters lap against the level fields; the clouds envelop the great earth.
Do not let that which lies to the left of my East Mountain rot away."
The furnace was opened. The various patriarchs were enshrined in the new Patriarchs’ Hall, and the Abbot ascended the hall to express thanks to the Supervisor of the Storehouse.
"In the south, at the head of the hearth, there is a saying regarding 'no guest and no host. Many have raised it in various quarters, and not few have understood it.
Our monastic community also has a version of this saying, which I shall present to you all. It is intended only that everyone may thoroughly comprehend it. Now tell me: what is this saying? Liang.
Jiuyun said: "The various halls have been restored; the ancestral patriarchs have their shrines.
On the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday, he ascends the hall. The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life; the greatest treasure of the Sage is called his station.
Most great and most firm, most supreme and most noble—let the peaks of Mount Song resound with cries of 'Ten-thousand Years!'"
Ascending the hall: All day long in a state of bustle, yet that matter remains unimpeded. Manifested yet not revealed; hidden yet not concealed.
What is this matter that is not concealed? The jade plum forms fruit upon the green tree; the stone sprout sends forth shoots above the green window.
Ascending the hall on the day of the Start of Spring: The spring mountains and spring waters flow; On this spring day, they strike the spring ox.
If you understand it as a "spring mood," Spring is not found in the forest retreats. If you do not understand it as a "spring mood," Spring colors fill the imperial capital.
Striking the whisk, he says: "Look, look! Good things begin once more."
Ascending the hall on the Sage’s Birthday: Wind-swept and rain-washed, the rocks remain moist; the waters are azure and the mountains bright, the heavens are even clearer.
Ten billion Mount Sumerus dance together, and throughout the great trichiliocosm, all voices raise a cry of joy. Do you all see this marvel?
After a long silence, he said: "Only the people find their lord.
Upon returning from the collection of tribute money in Hangzhou, he ascended the hall and said: "If the mind is free of affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise.
Yesterday, when I returned from Hangzhou, I obtained a staff with which to settle matters of state. But tell me, everyone: where is it?"
At the place of no affairs, after a long silence, he said: "The sound of the spring reaches its end at the pond; the mountain colors appear more fully upon the tower.

He ascended the hall and said: "The silkworms ascend to the baskets; the wheat is piled on the threshing floor. It is neither cold nor warm; the nights are short and the days are long. Principle and phenomena are not two."
The illumination and function are fully manifest. But tell me: as for the old farmer in the fields before the mountain, which son is he? *Pause.* He ascends the hall and cites Master Sidam:
"During the long summer retreat, I sat in meditation, majestic and unmoving. An attendant monk said, "Today is the day of *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults).
Sidam sighed to himself and said, "When the Buddha was in the world, those who realized the Way were countless. Today, the Sage has departed..."

He traveled ever further, yet gained nothing at all. Eventually, while he was reclining with his body relaxed, his faculty of sight suddenly became pure, and he beheld the entire trichiliocosm as clearly as if looking into the palm of his hand.
A verse says: "The autumn sky ten thousand miles away, a northwest wind blows; Pure as an ancient well, it mirrors the autumnal countenance.
Who among them possesses the eye that pierces through the thicket? Only one who recognizes the General’s merit of horses sweating in battle."
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: Two thousand years ago, Śākyamuni Buddha established three articles of law: "To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery;
with body and mind dwelling in peace, the wisdom of universal equality; practicing and realizing this within a fixed period, taking the wax figure as the test."
It is always a matter of strenuous exertion. Here, I simply maintain a state of leisurely detachment, doing nothing at all. Why?
Because while I am well-versed in the teachings of Liu Xiaohui, I ultimately do not take his outward traces as my model.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] thanked Chief Seat Shuping and Secretary Zhushui. Within pearls and stones there are gems, yet their brilliance shines from the depths;
within the monastic groves there are dragons and elephants, and thus the Buddha-Dharma flourishes. Leading disciples on pilgrimage does not preclude sitting together to deliberate;
sharing the seat to uphold the essential principles immediately makes one a source of vision for gods and men. To thoroughly penetrate Yunmen’s reception of Dongshan is to transcend...
That fierce tiger sits blocking the road; I, an old man among the mountain thickets, have another entrustment. Throwing down his staff, he said:
"The essential point lies in bearing the burden across one's shoulders."
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: Today is the eighth day of the fourth month, the anniversary of the World-Honored One’s birth.

Everywhere, they all perform the ritual of threefold ablution and threefold incense-offering. Although Yunfeng’s embodiment of naturalness is the same [as others], his application of it remains distinct.

He then took up his whisk and made a gesture of scooping, using the first ladle of water from the Tiger-Paw Spring to wash away the one who pointed to heaven and earth and falsely claimed self-exaltation. He then took up the whisk...
Disciple, make the gesture of scooping. With the second ladle, take one scoop of spring water and wash him—him who for nineteen years has preached both horizontally and vertically.

Again, take the whisk and make the gesture of scooping; with this third ladle of the eight meritorious waters, I scoop it out for you all and together proceed to the Great Hero’s Jewel Hall to wash him as he currently stands bare-bodied in the golden basin.
[He] struck the whisk and said: "To offer this body and mind to every dust-mote world—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "The tortoise was forced to reveal its markings; Bodhidharma came to Liang. People were led into the weeds; Kāśyapa Mātanga entered Han.
Before I had even entered my mother’s womb, I was already with all of you upon the long benches, eating porridge together and eating rice together."
Arising together with delusion: this morning, striking the board for seated meditation out of nowhere is like drawing water and setting fire.
On the Dragon Boat Festival, ascending the hall, one person gathers the medicine, while another administers it. But tell me, which one is the one who takes the medicine?
After a long silence, he said: "Sleeping soundly, one does not know the mountain rain has passed; having awakened, the palace halls are naturally cool.
Regarding wind and rain, when ascending the hall: it cannot be sought through a mind of non-existence, nor can it be attained through a mind of existence. To avoid the calamity of the wind and rain.
Furthermore, he encountered the calamity of water. He said to the assembly: "When traveling at night, do not step on white. He planted his staff and descended from the seat.
He offered thanks to the head monk of Daimei’s Zhitang Hall. Ascending the hall, he said: "That which is 'this very mind is Buddha'—the Yuyang Monastery has śarīra relics.
That which is 'neither this mind nor Buddha'—the Yuelin Monastery has Maitreya. That which is 'not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing'—Potalaka has Avalokiteśvara."
[He makes a sound. Holding up the whisk, he says: "Do you all see the Three Buddhas turning the Great Dharma Wheel atop this whisk?
Hanging down the whisk, he says: "If one were truly the Eye and Standard of humanity and heavens, they would have already discerned and seen through it."
Small Assembly for the Closing of Retreat: The entire earth is this very self; where, then, does one dwell? Taking all ten directions as a single monastery, how can one restrict one's steps?
Standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high, lift your head and smash through empty space, proceeding directly forward without hesitation, taking each step with confidence.
Transverse and vertical, intersecting like a cross—vast and open, utterly devoid of cultivation or realization. Who else could provide verification?
Even a wax figure would have nothing to testify to. It is so direct that Jinge Peak nods its head, saying "Yes, yes," and Hupao Spring breaks into laughter, "Ha ha!
But as for Dayu’s "stalk of radish" and Tianping’s "both were wrong"—how can this be discussed? (He strikes the whisk. I shall deliberate with you gently and at leisure.

Winter Solstice. Holding up his staff, he said: "All Tathāgatas of the past have already used it; all Bodhisattvas of the present are using it now; and those who practice and study in the future shall use it.
Here with me, it is not like that at all. This winter the crops are ripe; old debts are melted away.
The granaries are full and the rice baskets are not empty. It does no harm to serve a full platter high upon the table; thus, I unfold this teaching in full accordance with the season."
Regarding the family tradition: one immediately beholds Cloud Peak Pavilion and Subduing Tiger Rock.

They congratulate one another, join their palms at their chests, and whisper together, saying, "If we obtain two harvests in a single year, the Sangha Hall and Dharma Hall may then begin construction. This is indeed so.

As for the application of this very night, is it different from or the same as that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old? [He] strikes the meditation staff and says: "When the meaning emerges, the harvest is bountiful.
At the commencement of the summer retreat, the scorching sun blazes and the cool breeze blows gently. At such a time as this, the Yellow-Faced Old Man once used his whisk—
[The Master] struck a circle and said: "Take this net and cast it across the four quarters of the world to scoop up all living beings.
This is called 'restraining the feet to protect life' and 'attaining realization within a fixed period. Yet, more than two thousand years have passed and it has not been gathered in.
At this very site of the Dharma assembly, I shall now exert my strength to lift its main cord and pull its ropes; regardless of saint or ordinary person, I shall catch them all in one sweep. If...
Having already completed the thirty-six scales at the bottom, he strikes the whisk and says:
"Amidst this sound of a thunderclap, leap upward with a single bound and pass through the Yu Gate. If you have not yet done so, take care not to have your forehead marked."
Holding up an ancient precedent, he cited Master Tianyi Hui, who addressed the assembly, saying: "It is like a wild goose flying across the vast sky; its reflection sinks into the cold water.
The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no mind to retain the reflection."
The Master said: "O assembly, do you wish to see where the Venerable Tiandi’s four corners fell flat upon the ground?
The wild colors are no longer cut off by mountains; the light of heaven flows directly through to the waters."

Regarding the raising of National Teacher Niu: Whenever he prepared his own meals to provide for the assembly of monks, at every mealtime, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the Sangha Hall and perform a dance, saying, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat! He would then clap his hands and laugh loudly.
The Master said: "These are all merely playing with the breath of rice and gruel. Niu-tou, however, was a bit more capable.
He then cited Master Ren of Bai-shui, who addressed the assembly, saying: "Ordinarily, I do not wish to dally with people’s sons and daughters before sound or after a phrase.
Why is this? It is because sound is not sound, and form is not form. At that time, a monk asked: "As for..."
“What is sound that is not sound? Ren said, “Can you call it form? The monk asked, “What is form that is not form?
Ren said, “Can you call it sound? The monk bowed. Ren said, “Now tell me: did I speak for your sake, or did I answer your question?
If anyone can discern this, I grant them an entrance.”
The Master said, "A private merchant haggles over his wares; White Water urgently seeks someone to take charge.
He struck the whisk and said, "This is not sound; I speak it for you. He held up the whisk and said, "This is not form; I answer your question for you.
Even if you could discern this, I would not yet grant that you have a point of entry."
The Master cited the public case concerning the Three Sages’ question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat?
The Master said, “This blind donkey lets loose the golden fish that has passed through the net, intending to swallow up fifteen hundred people who are true spiritual friends.
Little does he realize that beneath the green silk banner, there is the mechanism of seizing and releasing; thus, one need not fight.”

And thus they subdue the enemy's troops. Although these two great elders are masters of their craft, displaying their skill with their own hands, for now they have not yet found a way to emerge from the path.
The National Teacher called to his attendant three times. Repeatedly summoning "Little Jade," there was originally no business at all.
The attendant responded three times; he simply wanted the patron to recognize the voice. I thought it was I who had failed you; I poured out my very liver and gall toward you.
Who would have known that it was you who had failed me? Acquaintances are just like strangers.
The Master said: "In this very place of practice, morning and evening, the moments of pecking and hatching coincide.
One should laugh at the National Teacher for 'exhausting his own mind'—laughing until he shatters the mouths of others."
An ancient worthy of the Verse School gave a small lecture: "He does not answer the question.

The beautiful woman drawing water stands in the morning breeze; her green silk rope is fully unwound and the well-sweep is empty; the silver pitcher is struck and shattered, leaving her makeup in disarray."
Fragrance. Falling petals reflect the red of the blossoms upon the water.
Master Quan of this mountain addressed the assembly, saying: "When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is gathered within it.
Why did Śākyamuni, the Old Man, contemplate such matters for twenty-one days? When a single flower blooms, the great..."
Dichun: "Master Dharma, for what reason did he face the wall for nine years?
If anyone can utter a word that brings the matter to a conclusion, they may sit and bring about a time of great peace."
The wind carries the fragrance of mountain flowers into my sleeves; with long days and nothing to do, I lean against my folding chair. The chaotic red petals fall like rain as spring departs;
the cuckoo cries out its song at every sunset.
An ancient worthy was once asked by a monk, "What is the teacher of all Buddhas? The Worthy replied, "Lately, Luzu has appeared in the world;
he speaks of the East when questioned about the West."

In the imperial gardens, the flowers have bloomed up to the peonies; the profusion of reds and purples brews a spring chill. To the eyes of the wandering travelers, there are no more Yao or Wei blossoms;
they can only gaze intently at the branches.
Master Benren addressed the assembly, saying: "One must not let sand enter the eyes; one must not let water enter the ears.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is 'not letting sand enter the eyes'? He replied, "The Peerless Perfected One.
The monk asked again, "What is 'not letting water enter the ears'? He replied, "White."
Pure and stainless;
beneath the thick shade of green trees, the summer days are long. The reflections of towers and terraces fall upon the broad pond. A light breeze stirs the crystal curtains;
the roses on every rack fill the entire courtyard with fragrance.
Master Pang points to the snow:
He points out into the void that white blur; how many streams of Chan practitioners have their eyesight withered!
Had he not struck him across the cheek with a single palm, he would have nearly frozen to death halfway there.
A Verse Sent to the Junior Disciple Duanqiao as He Returns to Yue to Dwell at Xie Fu’s Hermitage:
Broken clogs and trailing frost-colored horned caps lean askew; He establishes his livelihood on the banks of the King of Yue’s city. The son of the Xu family plants the seeds of the Xie family.
On the ground, sprouts emerge once more from the tips of the roots of the *xian* vegetable.
At Baiyun Hermitage, Master Ke remains thus:
coming and going in this way, dwelling in this way. The sky is clear and bright as the obscuring clouds disperse; one sits in meditation upon a patch of quietude.
Upon the stone, he broke off a pine branch to brush away the moss.
Drawing blood, he wrote the Lotus Sūtra;
beneath each finger-tip, he applied a needle. A red lotus first blossomed in the depths of the azure waves; a fragrant breeze blew, scattering the petals.
Relying on these, every single fragment is nothing other than a sincere heart.

When the former Chan guest (a native of Nanjian) questioned him, his words arose like clouds, impossible to restrain; his answers were like the waters of the Jian River surging against the current. He was able to turn his body around within the tiger’s den.
Go! I grant you that you have personally seen a single stroke of it.

Master Yishou took righteousness as his guiding cord and personally found the Way; with an iron heart, he did not let himself be altered by the changing seasons. In old age, both righteousness and the Way were forgotten.
Setting it aside, one wanders here by mountain and water’s edge.
A sea of poison surges, its scorching eyes ablaze as a murderous air arises; inverted black waves roll in layer upon layer—who knows that this transgression is most extreme?
The poison-crow: alive, it seizes the Kun and Jing to transform into the Peng bird.
At Cold Spring, the stone Buddha is gilded with gold. Assigned the rhyme "Shen," I write:
On Vulture Peak, the gibbons cry beneath the ancient trees' shade; the power to propagate the Image-Teaching lies in the present day. Big and small stones are all pure gold.
Wrapped up. At the end, on the single pivot, the mountain peaks subside.

Yutian (Jade Field) calls out with earnestness, carrying his uncut gem into the Master’s gate; yet traces of carving and polishing still remain. When the great earth is plowed over, not an inch remains.
The earth is vast and boundless; ten thousand qing of precious light shine with cold brilliance.
In praise of the late master, Venerable Jichuang.
My father called me "Weng," styling me Qu Tugai; my son now calls his father "Tong," styling him Qu Tutong. Do not take offense at this mutual exposure;
in principle, it is truly difficult to tolerate. Three dou of mugwort and three dou of scallions—swallowing and spitting them out, one must return them to the great old beast.

Zhongfeng was the king of three generations of barbarians; most poisonous was this World-Honored One of Compassion. He emerged from the herd of oxen at Guishan and plowed the ancestral fields of Dongshan.
At Qiyun, he was a purple灵芝 (lingzhi fungus); at Lingzhi, he was a rare jewel of the age. At Daoshan and Boshan, he ate the bitter ginseng root to its very core.
*Zha!* At Hongtang, he established a formidable fortress with deep moats and layered trenches; he spread his net across the heart of the river, where fish leaped and dragons rushed. He sat...

Leaning against the jade couch, he surveys heaven and earth; to those who approach, he strikes them across the spine and drags them away, leaving the patch-robed monks with no door through which to settle.
This is far superior to merely holding up a broken sand-pitcher.

To the Venerable Bahui: Regarding the scroll of the "Eulogy on Ancient Folly," it is said that the folly of antiquity was straightforward, while the folly of today is deceitful. You have taken the title "Ancient Folly"; is there not a profound purpose in this? Although...
However, you must further possess a resolute will and the eye of discernment; only then, when you settle this great matter with certainty, will you not fall short of the ancients.
Otherwise, you will fall into the tracks of the present age. Do not say that Yunfeng has not spoken the truth.
The attendant Neng’s verse on the scroll:
"The axis should have no place of abiding. One loses one's way in broad daylight; a foot slips at Huangmei. The Way is transmitted for a thousand ages.
Is it not that within the Great Tang there were no Chan masters, until this firewood-carrying fellow threw the four quarters of the world into turmoil? Attendant Neng, you are capable."
If one can be "recommended" [attained] while the firewood has not yet been cast off, it may be said that the task is complete.
If, however, you seek within this fascicle to see where Lu and Neng gained their power, then the single stream of Caoxi will sink into oblivion.
For this minor Buddhist rite, Assistant Attendant Ming lit the funeral pyre, saying:
"Possessing the mechanism of the 'peck' and the 'break,' he transcends the phrase of birth and death; with clarity as water and ice, he enters the great mass of fire."

The Master said to the attendant, "Yes. He threw down the fire and said, "When have I ever betrayed you? When Chief Seat Bing was about to pass away while sitting in meditation, he said, "It is not that there is no chief seat;

it is the old monk who must strike the ice to obtain the fire. He threw down the fire and said: [The Master] said to the attendant, "Yes. He threw down the fire and said, "When have I ever betrayed you? Chief Seat Bing sat in meditation and passed away. It is not that there is no chief seat; one must be an old monk like me to strike the ice and obtain the fire. He threw down the fire and said:
Even if one were to cast oneself across the three realms, one must still guard against the fierce flames leaping over the brow.
When Head Monk Song ate until he was nearly dead, Wuzu planted pine trees;
spring resides within the mattock. As the two halls let out a shout, thunder crashes upon dry land. Here, it can be overturned.
He exhaled his vital breath from his body; amidst the mass of fire and the mountain of blades, he played at will.

On the day the annual retreat began, he was able to carry firewood, move earth, and drag stones. When his tasks were completed, he happened upon the commencement of the retreat and immediately withdrew from his quarters. How could he have been willing to remain in strict seclusion and die there?
A cave. Nevertheless, one must further know the timing for turning the body. [The Master] threw down a firebrand and said, "This too is using fire to assist the heat.
Administrator Jeon (a native of Changheo who died at Xiechi).
Layered emeralds embrace the Qin River; what is there in this life’s conditions to cling to? Smoke and waters swell the Xi River; my dwelling place remains unsettled.
I ride backward upon a three-legged donkey, severing both ends at once. Although I am originally jade of the second rank, let me enter the fire to be tempered.

At the Temple of Official Fire on Mount Tashan, the fire-tower towers high and the bright moon shines clear. One buries one’s head amidst piles of paper money; before the stand of the bright mirror, one loses one’s reflection.

"O [person], I shall now give you a glimpse for you to examine," he said, and cast down a cloud of fire. "If you can discern it before good and evil are distinguished, the thousand peaks will dawn as the clouds of fire have entirely dispersed."
Dongtang Master Shipo Holds the Torch (Verse on Passing Away; containing the line: "Coming with no trace"):

Though the place of attainment is the same, the application differs. At the ultimate pivot beyond the gate, he revitalized the ancestral wind. With successive layers of steep mechanisms, he poured forth the Three Gorges.
Birth, death, coming, and going are but his playful sport. The late Great Master Shipo, former abbot of this mountain, whose fame was weighty in both [realms].

In the morning, the Way was transmitted through the ages. At eleven locations, using both gentle and fierce fires, he shattered the core of Wuzhun, causing the flames to erupt from dead wood and illuminate the Dragon Abyss.
For eighty-seven years, he enjoyed the longevity of old age; his capacity equaled that of the Elder Zeng.
He toppled the City of Nirvana and trampled the Tiger’s Den. It may be said that he came without a trace, like the moon moving through the sky, and departed [without a trace].
Yet there is nothing; it is like water rushing into a ravine, moving in an instant. A thousand ravines stir with wind, and the void stands abruptly prominent—his countenance is majestic and imposing.
Nevertheless, this is still the old monk’s final word as he departs, which has already been explained in detail.
But as for that very last phrase: do you all hear it being uttered right now? [He held up a torch.]
He drew a circle and said: "A rock stands in the void; fire burns within water.
End of the Recorded Sayings.
Compiled and verified by Ruxun, former Abbot of Guanghua Chan Temple.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Venerable Longyuan, Engraved by Zheng Ren of Wulin.
Composed by Mou Yan, Former Court Gentleman with Rank of Grand Master, Administrator of the Qianqiu Hongxi Observatory.

Written by Zhao Mengfu, Rectified Scholar of the Academy of Worthies (Jixian Zhixueshi), Court Rank of Great Officer (Chaolie Dafu), serving as the Director of Education for Jiangzhe and other regions, and inscribed with his own seal-script title.
This was in the seventh month of the year Yisi, five years after the passing of Chan Master Longyuan of Daochang Mountain. Written by his secretary (jiji).
Huaizhu compiled the master’s remaining deeds and, accompanied by his disciple Xiwei, came to request an inscription for the Heart-Source Stūpa (Xinyuan-ta).
I still recall that in the year Jiawu, I visited the Master at Yunfeng; I stayed for three days, exploring its secluded depths to my heart's content, feeling great joy.
Seven years later, I returned there once more with Deng Shanzhi, who was then a Court Editor (Huanlin Xiuzhuan). Upon seeing my face, the Master was delighted and accommodated me.
On a high pavilion, we brewed tea and conversed of old times; through the night, neither showed any sign of weariness. The next day, as we descended the mountain, we held hands as if unable to part.
Little did we expect that it would turn out to be a final farewell. Master Liugeng, Duke Wang Boda, was a renowned statesman of the former dynasty.
I shared the same aspirations for loyalty and righteousness with the late Sancha (Sang Cheong). Our discussions were identical, and our hearts and livers were one.
Furthermore, I was fortunate enough to form a friendship with his son and nephew. Since Master [Seo] was a member of the Gong clan, his earnest devotion toward me was as such.

How could I decline to compose this inscription? The Master’s name was Gyecheong; his courtesy name was Noryun. His family had resided in Changheok, Fuzhou, for generations. His grandfather’s name was Ik-gi. Gu...
[The Master’s] surname was Tian and his courtesy name was Xianwei. His father, Liangfu, served as the Magistrate of Huangyan County. His mother was Lady Cai, who had long been fond of doing good.

She once dreamed that a divine being, appearing in formal attire, presented her with a son, saying, "This is a virtuous teacher (śāstrā) who shall be born into your family. Indeed, she conceived and gave birth to the Master. From childhood, he abstained from meat and pungent roots.

At the age of seven, he delighted in reading Buddhist scriptures; as he grew older, his understanding became increasingly profound and enlightened. He read widely across the classics, histories, and the works of the hundred schools of thought.
His father, recognizing that he was no ordinary man, sent him to the Xuefeng Monastery in the prefecture to renounce the household life.

After residing there for half a year, he set out on a pilgrimage across Feiyuan Ridge and arrived at Fazang in Yixing, where he received ordination under Chan Master Yifeng Qi. At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head and received full precepts;

thereafter, he traveled extensively to seek instruction from masters throughout the various regions. At that time, there were Shi-fan Yan of Jingci and Tui-geng Ning of Lingyin. Jìng... [text fragment]

In the mountains and at Xutang, there were many who were enlightened masters and men of long-standing virtue, all of whom vied with one another to welcome him. The Master stood tall and firm as a mountain;

his movements were dignified and composed, and his speech was refined and elegant. His will was not easily swayed by others. While traveling through Wuxing, he happened upon Daochang Monastery, where Dongsou Ying appointed him as the Director of Guests (*dianbin*).

After Dongsou, Wu Deng and Rong succeeded him; they immediately requested the Master to serve as the Internal Registrar (*neiji*), but he declined their offer with great persistence and crossed the river to depart.
He passed by King Ashoka’s stupa and went to pay his respects to Chan Master Jichuang Zhao, entering the inner quarters where he attained a realization of the Dharma.

He served as the attendant for the incense and subsequently took charge of the treasury keys. Jichuang had inherited the lineage from Kushan, and Kushan from Mian; they were all eminent figures from Southern Min.
The Master appeared in the world at Shouguo in Siming, and subsequently moved to Kaishou.

There was the Prefect Zhou, son of the Prime Minister Shi Du, who, seeing that the Master’s practice and realization were in perfect accord, relinquished his residence at the Kaishou provincial seat to provide for the Master’s retirement, naming it the Ximing Hermitage as a plan for his final years.
Before long, the seat of the monastic center became vacant, and the various mountains of the two Zhe regions nominated the Master; thus he came to this mountain. It was indeed...

Regarding the Tang-era temple: since the time of the Xi Ning era, when the Great Master Su visited Daochang and his various poems were published, its fame grew even more weighty among the Five Mountains.
Consequently, its selection for such status was no longer treated with levity or disregard. In the Bingzi year, the temple was consumed by the fires of destruction, reduced to rubble.
Ten years later, in the Yiyou year, the original splendor had not yet been restored. Once the Master arrived, he took it upon himself with deep resolve to rebuild what had fallen into ruin; first...
The Great Buddha Jewel Hall was completed, its golden and azure decorations resplendent and its sacred images magnificent.

Next, the Avalokiteśvara Treasury Hall was constructed, where the Great Tripitaka in five thousand and forty-eight fascicles was transcribed. Furthermore, the Sandalwood Forest, the Arrayed Verdant Pavilion, the Mōng Hall, the Dharma Hall, the Monks’ Hall, and the Practice Hall were established.
From the central area to the outer precincts, the drum-towers, bells, and ritual implements were all refurbished to a brilliant new state. IV.

At that time, monks from all quarters, having heard of the Master’s reputation, traveled with their bags slung over their shoulders and alms bowls in hand; their sleeves brushed against one another as they flocked together like clouds gathering and mist rising.
Consequently, his fame reached the imperial court, where he was received with profound honor.
By imperial decree, he was granted a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*.

Respectfully receiving this dharma instruction, he was further bestowed the title "Buddha-ocean Xingkong" (Xingkong of the Buddha-ocean), so that he might offer even a small measure of gratitude for what has been accomplished through his diligent cultivation of the bodhicitta.

On the third day of the sixth month in the year of Xinchou, he suddenly manifested a slight illness. He requested a bath and had his hair washed, then wrote a verse: “The Buddha sat for ten kalpas; I have sat for seventeen years.
Explaining the profound meaning of birth and death, There is neither before nor after between ancient and modern. He passed away with serene composure. It was the first heat of the summer (Gengfu).
His remains were kept in the shrine for seven days, yet his countenance and spirit remained unchanged. After the cremation, his cranial bone and teeth [remained intact].
He possessed a prayer bead rosary that never broke. He was sixty-three years of age and forty-eight years since his ordination.

He had ordained more than two hundred and fifty disciples; he now resides at Chongunsa Temple in Suyeon as its head monk. Originally, the temple lacked the three pagodas [of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha].
The Master felt this was a deficiency and spoke to his disciple Siji and others about planning their construction. He then donated his own wealth to purchase Mount Zhu.
To the east of the temple, three pagodas were constructed, and he requested that a funerary pagoda for his master be built alongside them.

Once the hermitage was completed, the Master inscribed its name as "Xinyuan" (Source of Mind). Zhi and others further gathered funds to purchase fields to provide for the expenses of incense and lamps.
He appointed a practitioner to serve as the attendant for sweeping and cleaning. When three years had passed, he ranked them according to their seniority;
the one who stood first was ordained as a monk and received the title of the current abbot, after which he performed the ritual of bowing at the stupa to honor his teacher.
Such were the regulations. Upon reaching this point, [the remains] were finally interred. Generally, it is said that all various Buddhist rites are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). This—

It is not yet necessary to discuss the source of the dragon; however, the establishment of that source likewise depends on what can be done according to the times, while exhausting all that ought to be done with one's strength—not acting for oneself.
Therefore, though there is activity throughout the year, it has never been a case of "acting.
If one insists that these are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and dismisses them all as non-action, then [one would contradict] Master Chengguan’s...
The Stūpa of the Saṃgha. Why did Lord Changli (Mencius) praise his public talent as surpassing that of other officials, yet lament that his numinous bones had already grown old?
The Master’s power of aspiration was indeed vast. The inscription says:
Descendant of Liugeng, heir to Mian’s tradition, He sat in meditation at Yunfeng for seventeen years.

Appearing when conditions were ripe, he departed as soon as they were exhausted; Suddenly, in a single day, like ice melting or a cicada shedding its shell, His nature was originally empty—neither perishing nor persisting.
This is the ocean of Buddha-nature, the source of the Dragon Spring.
Draw from it and it is never exhausted; it is without past or present. This is the Source of the Dragon.
Within the square inch of the mind, one establishes three pagodas, yet these four constitute the third. This is the True Abode. The hermitages of the source of the mind are each a site of practice;
they are nowhere not present. In every place, light is full, and there is no defilement or decay.
May you, his descendants, look upon these engraved words as if seeing your teacher for the first time; seek [the truth] from its source.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of autumn in the year of Great Virtue (Bǐyǐ), the disciple Xīwèi erected this stone.
Now, those who expound the Dharma are like rivers, streams, ponds, and marshes; their waves may be broad or narrow, and their sources and currents may be shallow or deep—truly, they are not the same.
Yet as for their flowing forth, they are all equally water. Observing now the proclamations of the Three Assemblies at Longyuan, one sees them to be profound, solemn, and vast;
this is because their branches and tributaries have flowed and spread from the Spirit’s Abyss. One can thus see how they submerge mountains and flood over the hills, surging forth in tide.
The heavens drench the sun; countless common people are submerged in the depths of the land.
On the day of the commencement of the retreat in the year of Great Virtue Bingwu, Tiantong Dongyan (Jingri), at the age of eighty-six, wrote this colophon.
